_expect.name: Mod Pod aka Phallic Rock, The

co_mod_pod_aka_phallic_rock_the.blurb: A single large, creek-side boulder in the Inner Canyon part of Castlewood Canyon State Park, south of Denver. About a dozen problems wrap its north, west and south faces, nearly all VB to V2, so it suits beginners or a quick warm-up circuit. Several of the lines are tall for the grade, so a pad and a spotter are worth bringing. The sunny face looks south, and the rock is sandstone. It is a short stroll from the trail, so it pairs well with a walk through the canyon rather than a full bouldering day.

co_east_buttress_3.blurb: A small mixed and alpine buttress on the Hallett Peak side of Rocky Mountain National Park, reached by heading past Emerald Lake from the Bear Lake side. It is a winter objective: easy drytooling and turf on scrappy rock that needs cold temperatures and some snow to feel solid, with no real ice. Most of the roughly eleven lines are M3 to M4, with a couple of M5 pitches and a few moderate rock grades. Avalanche exposure is low, which makes it a sensible place to learn trad mixed climbing or to climb when the weather is poor. Descents generally go down nearby couloirs.

co_revenge_area.blurb: This group of high-elevation problems sits midway up Lower Chaos Canyon in Rocky Mountain National Park, just east of the Bush Pilot and Gobot blocks. About eleven problems range from an easy V0 up to V8, with the bulk of them at the hard end of the spread and a handful of moderate lines, so it suits strong boulderers more than beginners. Landings are rough talus, which makes several pads close to essential. Snow lingers late into summer, so the usable season is short, and the area is fragile enough that care with chalk and vegetation matters.

co_squire_gulch.blurb: A small, quiet side drainage at the start of Cathedral Park, near Colorado Springs. A narrow gulch holds about a dozen short, fully bolted routes, nearly all of them sport, with a single trad line. Grades sit mostly in the 5.4 to 5.7 range with a lone hard 5.11 outlier, so it is well suited to beginners, families and small groups wanting an easy day. The climbs are short and simple by design, and most of the left-hand routes are reached from the top. Expect little company and a calm setting.

co_lost_highway_area.blurb: A remote, separate section at the far right end of Sleeping Beauty in Boulder Canyon, west of Boulder. Eleven routes mix mostly bolted sport lines with a couple of trad climbs and one top rope, and the grades run from a 5.8 up through plenty of 5.10 and 5.11 to a few 5.12s, so it is aimed at experienced climbers. One of the routes is a three-pitch bolted line, while the rest are single pitches of roughly 70 to 120 feet. The feel is more isolated than the main wall, and getting to the base takes some route-finding along ledges and a short rappel.

_expect.name: Milk Creek (aka Wolcott Entrada Band - East)

co_milk_creek_aka_wolcott_entrada_band_e.blurb: A small trad area on the lower red sandstone bands east of Milk Creek, a mostly dry wash near Wolcott in the Eagle River valley. All eleven routes are traditionally protected, short at roughly 50 to 90 feet, and mostly dihedrals following finger to hand cracks. Grades span about 5.7 to 5.12, with the weight on 5.11, so it favors competent crack climbers. The style recalls Utah desert crack climbing. It is a low-elevation spot reached by a short walk of around twenty minutes along the drainage.
co_milk_creek_aka_wolcott_entrada_band_e.approach: Leave the car at the Wolcott boulders area, follow the creek upstream through the campground, cross the trestle, then walk the tracks to the Milk Creek wash and take the trail on its east side.
